name: Uttal
subtitle: Pronunciation: vowels, long and short sounds, soft g and k

ruleCards.title: Nine vowels
ruleCards.rule: Swedish has nine vowels. A, o, u and å are hard vowels. E, i, y, ä and ö are soft (front) vowels, and they change how g, k and sk sound before them.
ruleCards.watch: Mouth tips: for y, make the mouth for u but say i. For ö, make the mouth for o but say e.

fun.sv: Svenska har nio vokaler. Jag kan säga sju av dem.
fun.en: Swedish has nine vowels. I can pronounce seven of them.
fun.note: For most English speakers the hard ones are y and u.

ruleCards.title: Long and short vowels
ruleCards.rule: A vowel before one consonant is long. A vowel before a double consonant (or two consonants) is short. Long vowel, short consonant; short vowel, long consonant.
ruleCards.watch: The length changes the meaning: tak is a roof, tack is thank you.

fun.sv: – Ett glas, tack! – Glas eller glass? – Ja, gärna båda.
fun.en: “A glass, please!” “A glass or an ice cream?” “Yes, both please.”
fun.note: Glas (a glass) has a long a; glass (ice cream) has a short a before the double s.

ruleCards.title: Soft g
ruleCards.rule: G before a soft vowel (e, i, y, ä, ö) sounds like j. Before a hard vowel (a, o, u, å) it stays hard.
ruleCards.watch: This happens in the stressed syllable, usually at the start of the word. In endings the g stays hard: dagen, vägen.

fun.sv: Gästen gillar att gå, men aldrig hem.
fun.en: The guest likes walking, but never home.
fun.note: Gäst and gillar start with a j sound (soft vowel after g); gå keeps a hard g.

ruleCards.title: Soft k
ruleCards.rule: K before a soft vowel (e, i, y, ä, ö) sounds like tj, a soft “ch” sound. Before a hard vowel it stays hard.
ruleCards.watch: A few common words break the rule: kille (guy) has a hard k.

fun.sv: Vi köper ett nytt kök, men katten gillar bara kartongen.
fun.en: We buy a new kitchen, but the cat only likes the cardboard box.
fun.note: Köper and kök start with the soft tj sound; katten and kartongen keep a hard k.

ruleCards.title: Soft sk
ruleCards.rule: Sk before a soft vowel (e, i, y, ä, ö) sounds like sh. Before a hard vowel it stays sk.

fun.sv: Skon är snygg men inte skön.
fun.en: The shoe looks nice but isn’t comfortable.
fun.note: Sko keeps a hard sk before o; skön starts with a sh sound before ö.

ruleCards.title: Tj, sj, skj: always soft
ruleCards.rule: Tj always sounds like tj. Sj, skj and stj always sound like sh, whatever vowel comes after.
ruleCards.watch: Words ending in -tion also have the sh sound: station, lektion.

fun.sv: Tjugo tjejer sjunger vid sjön. Fiskarna flyttar.
fun.en: Twenty girls are singing by the lake. The fish move out.
fun.note: Tj is always tj and sj is always sh, even before u and ö.

ruleCards.title: Rs and rt
ruleCards.rule: R + s blends into one sh sound. R + t (and r + d, r + n, r + l) blend into one sound with the tongue curled back.
ruleCards.watch: In Finland Swedish the r and the s are often said separately, so you will hear both.

fun.sv: Kursen i svenska är kort. Kaffepausen är längre.
fun.en: The Swedish course is short. The coffee break is longer.
fun.note: Rs in kursen is one sh sound; rt in kort is one sound with the tongue curled back.

ruleCards.title: Hj, dj, lj, gj: just j
ruleCards.rule: At the start of a word, the h, d, l or g in hj, dj, lj and gj is silent. The word starts with a j sound.

fun.sv: Mitt hjärta säger ja, men min plånbok ropar på hjälp.
fun.en: My heart says yes, but my wallet is calling for help.
fun.note: In hjärta and hjälp the h is silent: both start with a plain j sound.

ruleCards.title: Stress: kaffe or kafé?
ruleCards.rule: Most Swedish words are stressed on the first syllable. Many words from French are stressed on the last syllable, often a syllable with é.
ruleCards.watch: Kaffe (KAF-fe) is the drink, kafé (ka-FÉ) is the place.

fun.sv: Jag beställde ett kafé. Servitören gav mig nycklarna.
fun.en: I ordered a café. The waiter gave me the keys.
fun.note: Stress changes the word: KAFfe is coffee, kaFÉ is a café.
